title: The Robert H. Lurie Comprehensive Cancer Center
text: The Robert H. Lurie Comprehensive Cancer Center of Northwestern University (NU) is an NCI-designated, comprehensive matrix cancer center conducting a broad range of multidisciplinary clinical, basic, translational and population science research. Our core mission is to reduce the burden of cancer across all populations. Our researchers conduct cutting-edge, paradigm-shifting science, and we continually strive to develop translational paths for scientific discoveries that will ultimately reduce the burden of cancer for patients in our catchment area, nationally and worldwide.

title: Artifact-free Micro-LED Optoelectrode for Multi-color Neuromodulation
text:
This project will develop and validate large-scale optoelectrodes for analysis of dynamic activity of neural
circuits at cellular resolution in a behaving animal. The number of neuron-sized micro LEDs will be directly
integrated on the probe shank close to high-density recording sites and further scaled up and extended to
multi-color illumination to allow cellular resolution in cell-type specific stimulation. The developed tool will be
validated in animal experiments to monitor temporal precision of neuronal assemblies in memory and
differentiate neuronal responses to external inputs against intrinsic mechanisms, which is critical to understand
and study neural disease and disorders.

title: Ultrasound Imaging Biomarkers of Crohn's Disease
text:
Crohn’s Disease (CD) is a chronic inflammatory bowel condition that affects over 1 million Americans, with
associated costs exceeding hundreds of billions of dollars. Frequent and accurate imaging follow-ups are
crucial for guiding therapy. In this study, we aim to develop and test a new ultrasound technology designed for
safe, cost-effective, and accurate evaluation of Crohn’s disease, enabling frequent assessments to guide
treatment adjustments.

title: Structural and dynamic basis for PRKACA-dependent signalopathies
text:
The PRKACA gene encodes for the catalytic subunit of protein kinase A. Genetic sequencing
identified mutations in the catalytic subunit of kinase A linked to adenoma-associated Cushing’s
syndrome, cardiac myxomas, fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinomas, and intraductal oncocytic
papillary neoplasms of the pancreas and bile ducts. We will identify the molecular mechanisms
underlying these dysfunctional kinases, paving the way for alternative and innovative therapies.

title: Investigating the impact of disease-associated mutations in the Polycomb system
text:
Our work will advance current knowledge into how specific missense mutations in RING1 and RNF2 genes affect
PRC1 activity, chromatin interaction, gene regulation and neurogenesis in vivo and in vitro. It will also shed light
on the role of PRC1 in neurodevelopmental disorders, enhancing our understanding of the complex interplay
between epigenetic mechanisms and neurodevelopment.

title: The impact of adolescent stress on neural circuits underlying punishment resistant reward seeking
text:
Chronic stress in adolescence alters how the brain processes rewards later in life, biasing individuals towards
addictive-like behaviors. However, the specific changes induced by stress remain unknown. This project will
answer fundamental questions about how stress in adolescence alters a circuit projecting from the amygdala to
midbrain dopamine neurons, suggesting a potential focus for treatment and prevention of addictive disorders.

title: Peptide-conjugated phosphodiamidate morpholino oligonucleotide (PPMO)-based henipavirus therapeutics
text:
Nipah viruses cause severe disease in humans and are therefore a public health threat, but no antiviral therapies
are available to treat Nipah virus infections. This project addresses this need by developing peptide-conjugated
phosphorodiamidate morpholino oligomers (PPMO) that inhibit Nipah virus replication.

title: Mechanisms underlying increased risk of hematological malignancy in sickle cell disease.
text:
Sickle cell disease (SCD) is an inherited red blood cell disorder that changes their shapes to bizzare
hook/sickle shapes that occlude blood vessels and have shortened lifespan, causing painful events and
anemia and contribute to chronic organ damage and mortality. More recently, patients with SCD been
observed to have a higher incidence of blood cancers, especially after gene therapy and bone marrow stem
cell transplantation. We want to study the underlying mechanism of increased blood cancers in SCD using
deep sequencing of leukemia associated genes in bone marrow DNA of SCD mice and normal mice as they
age, or when they are transplanted, to model this experimentally and develop targeted therapies.

title: Advancing Approaches to Identify Young Children at Risk for Post-Discharge Mortality
text:
Post-hospital discharge mortality rates among young children aged <5 years in sub-Saharan Africa are as high
as 3-18%, far outpacing the 0.1% rate we recently described in US children. Despite this immense disparity,
there are currently no externally validated or implemented risk assessment tools to identify young children at
risk for post-hospital discharge mortality in sub-Saharan Africa. The proposed research will assess the
discriminatory ability of machine learning risk assessment tools for post-hospital discharge mortality, includes
the first external validation study of risk assessment tools for post-hospital discharge mortality among young
children in sub-Saharan Africa, and will elucidate the role of a novel biomarker of endothelial dysfunction to
predict post-hospital discharge mortality among young children.

title: Ecological niche assignment in the gut microbiome on an ecosystem-level scale
text:
The human gut microbiome is a complex microbial ecosystem which impacts health in a myriad of ways. The
proposed studies seek to determine the adaptations that allow different microbes to coexist within the gut.
Results from these studies will advance a basic understanding of the gut microbiome and could clarify the
significance of changes in the microbiome that occur in various diseases.

title: Early developmental mechanisms of Rett Syndrome
text:
Rett Syndrome is a devastating neurodevelopmental disorder which primarily affects girls, and is
caused by mutations in the MECP2 gene. We propose to examine early deficits in cortical
neurogenesis and neuronal migration caused by MECP2 mutations, as a way to understand
fundamental changes in brain development in Rett Syndrome. These findings will help develop
therapeutics targeting these early developmental stages.

title: The role of T-type calcium channels in the morphine effects in the nonspecific thalamus
text:
Alterations in the nonspecific thalamus, a brain region crucial for consciousness, are recently implicated in the
morphine effects and addictive disorders. Thus, resolving the mechanisms that regulate its activity is an
important task in the pursuit of novel drug targets. This research proposal will provide the first comprehensive
study on the role of T-type calcium channels in the nonspecific thalamus in the function of the morphine-mediated
effects and opioid addiction, using ex vivo recordings of neuronal activity and behavioral experiments, coupled
with a sophisticated genetic approach, thereby identifying these channels as a potential drug target for opioid
use disorder.

title: Genomic control of gene regulatory networks governing early human lineage decisions
text:
(RELEVANCE) - No Change from Initial Application
 This project will construct models of gene regulatory networks controlling early human development by
taking an integrative approach involving perturbation of core regulatory network elements, quantitative
genomic and proteomic measurements with high temporal and single-cell resolution, and systems level
analyses. Knowledge gained from the study will provide a conceptual framework for dissecting gene regulatory
networks during cell state transitions, and reveal general features of genomic variants that contribute to cellular
and organismal phenotypes.

title: The genomic basis of environmental adaptation in house mice
text:
A central challenge in biology is to understand the genetic basis of complex traits, including those relevant for
human health. Genes underlying human metabolic disorders show variation that correlates with climate,
suggesting a link between environmental adaptation and disease. Mice are the premier model for humans,
and the proposed work will describe the genetic basis of complex traits underlying environmental adaptation in
mice.

title: Computational Pathology of Proteinuric Diseases
text:
The computer vision technologies and machine learning methods applied in this grant will
facilitate a precision medicine approach for nephrotic syndrome patients through automated
histologic assessment of renal biopsies and comprehensive characterization of kidney structure,
function, and molecular endophenotypes. The computational pathology framework and
understanding of biology and disease trajectory will serve as a support tool to guide pathologists
and nephrologists in kidney research, clinical trials, and clinical care for proteinuric
glomerulonephropathies.

title: Optogenetic Control of Bacterial Persistence to Study Biomaterial Infections
text:
Bacterial persister cells are phenotypic non-growing variants that play important roles in chronic infections and
facilitate the development and wide spread of bacterial multidrug resistance. This project aims to develop an
optogenetic system and an animal model for controlling and monitoring persister formation in vivo, which are
useful for fundamental studies of persister formation and for development of new control agents. Thus, it has
significance in infection control, which is critical to public health.

title: CardioPulmonary Vascular Biology COBRE
text:
The vision of the CardioPulmonary Vascular Biology (CPVB) COBRE program is to develop effective approaches
to prevent and treat vascular diseases affecting the pulmonary and cardiovascular systems through better
understanding of disease mechanisms. This will be accomplished by serving as an interdisciplinary center which
promotes collaborative research and provides excellent technical support and resources to investigators. The
overall mission of the CPVB COBRE program has been to build the human and technical infrastructure and
services that serve as catalysts to increase research in cardiopulmonary vascular biology in the state.

title: A wearable orthogonal ultrasound array for continuous imaging of the heart
text:
The proposed project aims to address the limitations of current cardiac imaging techniques by developing a
wearable ultrasound imager for continuous, non-invasive monitoring of the heart. This technology has the
potential to revolutionize the field of cardiac imaging by providing direct and real-time assessment of cardiac
functions, which may lead to early detection and improved management of cardiovascular diseases and acute
conditions. The development of this wearable technology has the potential to greatly benefit the field of critical
care and expand the possibilities for cardiovascular disease management.

title: Dual action immunostimulatory nanoparticles for treatment of aggressive cancers
text:
We seek to design a potent dual action immunostimulatory nanoparticle that reprograms and activates the
innate immune cells because these cells recruit systemic immunity. Such approach can facilitate an antitumor
immune response leading to tumor rejection and prevention of disease relapse.

title: Light Microscopy Facility Core
text: LIGHT MICROSCOPY FACILITY (LMF) CORE PROJECT SUMMARY Recent innovations in microscopy, including confocal and light-sheet microscopy, have extended microscopic analysis to 3D imaging of whole model organisms and the generation of comprehensive data on tissue structure, mRNA and protein expression, and fluorescent reporters of cell behavior in vivo. The MDIBL Light Microscopy Facility (LMF) Core will support graduated COBRE Project Leaders and other Davis Center investigators as well as the Maine INBRE and the greater IDeA network. This will be done through providing access to cutting edge lightsheet microscopy as well as support, training, and education in microscopy and digital image analysis. The LMF CORE, managed by Dr. Frederic Bonnet, will offer Core-assisted use of a newly constructed mesoSPIM for selective plane illumination microscopy (SPIM) that generates high resolution, wide field of views and complete 3D images of fixed cleared biological tissue. The aim of this COBRE LMF CORE proposal is to offer MDIBL and IDeA state investigators assisted use of the mesoSPIM in our Light Microscope Core facility that will support innovation in imaging and provide education in image acquisition, tissue clearing, and image processing and analysis. The LMF CORE will also hire a bio-imaging data scientist to design and establish image analysis pipelines, keep up to date with the latest analysis tools, aid in data submission to national repositories in keeping with current data management plan requirements, and support a growing base of users. The MDIBL Light Microscopy Facility Core has taken a leadership role in a developing a statewide microscopy network by establishing a microscopy course at MDIBL for graduate students, post-docs, research assistants, and faculty from institutions across Maine. The COBRE LMF CORE will also organize and host two imaging workshops highlighting 1) recent advances in biological imaging and innovations in light-sheet microscopy and 2) innovations in genetically encoded biosensors and digital image analysis. The COBRE LMF CORE will also fund a visiting scientist program to enable investigators to use MesoSPIM imaging in their projects by providing travel grants and user fee waivers. Enabling visiting investigators to acquire imaging data for publication and grant applications will extend the impact of the COBRE Light Microscopy Facility Core to IDeA states nationally.
